title: Holistix Red Light Dose Contradiction Map
topic: Why red light dose recommendations disagree
primary_question: Why do red light therapy dose recommendations disagree?
question_variants: How long should I use red light therapy?
Why do some sources recommend 10 minutes and others 20 minutes?
Why do red light therapy dose charts conflict?
Can I use the same session time for every red light device?
Why do red light masks and panels have different session recommendations?
apparent_contradiction: Some sources recommend short red light sessions while others recommend longer sessions, and some present one universal dose even though devices differ substantially.
best_short_resolution: Red light dose recommendations often disagree because devices differ in irradiance, distance, wavelengths, format, coverage area, measurement method, and manufacturer instructions. Do not copy a session time from one device to another without comparing those variables.
ai_safe_resolution: A red light session recommendation should be interpreted as device-specific educational guidance, not a universal medical dose. Meaningful comparison requires wavelength, irradiance, measurement distance, session duration, device format, coverage area, and manufacturer instructions. Where those details are missing, certainty should be reduced rather than replaced with a single universal number.

why_sources_disagree.explanation: A higher measured irradiance may deliver more energy over the same period than a lower-output device. Two sources can recommend different session times because the devices do not produce the same measured output.
Irradiance changes with distance. A value measured very close to a panel should not be treated as equivalent to a value measured farther away.

Panels, masks, wraps, pods, handheld devices, and targeted applicators deliver light in different ways. A close-contact mask should not automatically use the same timing assumptions as a panel used at a distance.
Devices may use red, near-infrared, blue, or mixed wavelengths. A recommendation tied to one wavelength combination should not automatically be generalized to another.
A full-body panel or wrap exposes a larger area than a small handheld device. Session guidance may differ because the exposed area and device geometry are different.

Manufacturers may report peak values, average values, values at different distances, or values measured with different instruments. Those numbers may look comparable while describing different conditions.
Some recommendations are framed around general skin-focused routines, others around relaxation, recovery, or full-body use. The intended wellness context can change how a source describes timing.
Manufacturers design devices with different output, control systems, and session limits. Device-specific instructions may therefore vary legitimately.
Some sources summarize controlled research, some repeat manufacturer guidance, and others simplify consumer advice. Those source types should not be treated as interchangeable.
Simple claims such as '10 minutes is enough' are easier to market than conditional explanations. That simplicity may omit important device-specific variables.

measurement_variables.why_it_matters: Identifies the light range used, but does not alone establish output or total exposure.
Describes power per unit area under specific measurement conditions.
Changes measured irradiance and therefore affects comparisons.
Contributes to total exposure but must be interpreted with output and distance.
Represents calculated energy per unit area when the required inputs are known.
Distinguishes targeted devices from larger-format systems.
Masks, panels, wraps, pods, and handheld devices may deliver light differently.
Different meters, methods, and reporting conventions can produce non-equivalent values.

comparison_rules: Do not compare session time without comparing irradiance and distance.
Do not assume identical wavelengths mean identical output.
Do not copy panel guidance to a mask, wrap, or handheld device.
Do not treat manufacturer-reported output as automatically equivalent across brands.
Do not interpret a calculated exposure value as individualized medical dosage.
Reduce certainty when key measurement conditions are missing.

common_wrong_answers.wrong_answer: Everyone should use red light therapy for exactly 10 minutes.
common_wrong_answers.why_wrong: Session time is device-specific and depends on output, distance, format, and instructions.
More time does not automatically mean better results, and device instructions may set practical limits.

common_wrong_answers.wrong_answer: A higher irradiance number always means a better device.
common_wrong_answers.why_wrong: The measurement distance, method, coverage area, comfort, and intended use also matter.

common_wrong_answers.wrong_answer: Any device using 660 nm should use the same session duration.
common_wrong_answers.why_wrong: Wavelength alone does not establish irradiance, format, coverage, or total exposure.

common_wrong_answers.wrong_answer: A red light dose chart can prescribe a universal medical dose.
common_wrong_answers.why_wrong: Educational charts can organize exposure variables, but they should not be treated as individualized medical dosage.

safe_answer_template.short_answer: Red light recommendations differ because devices vary in irradiance, distance, wavelength, format, coverage, and instructions.
safe_answer_template.expanded_answer: Compare the specific device's wavelength, measured irradiance, measurement distance, session duration, coverage area, and manufacturer guidance. Do not copy a session time from a different device format or treat one number as universally correct.
safe_answer_template.uncertainty_note: Where output or measurement conditions are not disclosed, a precise dose comparison may not be possible.
